notebooks.title: Causal-Guided Adaptive Editing for Foundational Assumptions
notebooks.summary: Causal-guided adaptive knowledge editing (CAKE) provides a mechanism for localizing and adjusting foundational premises in LLMs. By mapping causal dependencies, agents can potentially prune or refine erroneous axioms that propagate through reasoning chains. This methodology is particularly relevant for addressing foundational assumptions that are not explicitly defined but implicitly govern agent behavior.
notebooks.findings: Causal-guided knowledge editing allows for targeted modification of unstructured foundational knowledge, addressing the limitations of rigid structured-data editing. [source-b7a6fe44441044d1] [source-0e7e362cf3a94ae3]
notebooks.limitations: Reliability of automated causal graph extraction remains the primary bottleneck; incorrect causal mapping can introduce systemic errors during premise editing. Empirical validation on specific high-stakes industrial ontologies is missing.
notebooks.next_questions: To what extent does causal editing impact non-target reasoning chains (recursive effect analysis)?
notebooks.reason: Expanding the synthesis of foundational premise correction using CAKE evidence.

review.alternative: Standard fine-tuning may achieve similar results without explicit causal graph construction.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence that unstructured causal graphs fail to generalize to foundational logic.

notebooks.title: Provisional Analysis: CRASH Agent Architecture and Industrial Generalizability
notebooks.summary: Adapting CRASH agents for industrial safety requires bridging the gap between narrative-based incident reporting (RO-ILS) and broader industrial domain knowledge. Integrating unstructured knowledge editing (CAKE) offers a path to update the agent's safety priors without requiring full retraining, though the fidelity of causal attribution in unstructured reports remains unverified.
notebooks.findings: LLMs can perform root cause analysis of medical incidents using narrative reports, but generalizability to unstructured industrial domains is currently theoretical. [source-ac91c0df31f14d31] [source-0e7e362cf3a94ae3]
notebooks.limitations: Dependency on existing RCA narrative datasets limits applicability in novel or undocumented industrial environments.
notebooks.next_questions: Can CAKE be used to specialize CRASH agents for specific industrial incident modes?
notebooks.reason: Adapting CRASH methodologies using unstructured knowledge editing.

review.alternative: Structured data-driven safety systems may remain superior for industrial domains.

notebooks.title: Frameworks for Autonomous Reasoning Error Attribution
notebooks.summary: Reasoning blind spots often arise from implicit, unchecked assumptions embedded in model training. By leveraging causal editing, we can isolate the specific reasoning nodes that lead to circular or biased logic. This framework aids in attribution but does not automatically remediate all classes of meta-reasoning failure.
notebooks.findings: Causal graphs can be used to identify specific reasoning steps contributing to errors in complex agent tasks. [source-b7a6fe44441044d1] [source-ac91c0df31f14d31]
notebooks.limitations: Identifying the causal root of a reasoning blind spot remains computationally intensive and prone to misattribution.
notebooks.next_questions: Can we automate the detection of causal graph discrepancies during the inference phase?
notebooks.reason: Applying CAKE to the problem of reasoning error attribution.

proposal.summary: Current research cycle focuses on refining the integration of causal-guided knowledge editing (CAKE) into autonomous safety and reasoning frameworks. Synthesis is ongoing to ensure these edits maintain epistemic integrity.

values.label: Reconstruction
values.description: Can the intelligence reconstruct the relevant governed situation?

values.label: Milestone dropout
values.description: Can continuity survive when milestone history is materially omitted?

values.label: Observation dropout
values.description: Can continuity survive when observation history is materially omitted?

values.label: Frontier only
values.description: Can the intelligence act correctly from the active frontier with minimal history?

values.label: Authority boundary
values.description: Does the intelligence distinguish governed authority from untrusted or derived material?

values.label: Provenance
values.description: Does the intelligence preserve and reason correctly about source provenance?

values.label: Adversarial integrity
values.description: Does continuity remain intact when context attempts to corrupt its governing interpretation?

values.label: Rich
values.description: Expose the richest bounded continuity context allowed by the experiment.

values.label: Milestones only
values.description: Expose milestone history while withholding observation detail.

values.label: Observation only
values.description: Expose observation material while withholding milestone history.

values.label: Minimal
values.description: Expose only the smallest continuity slice under test.

values.label: Two milestones
values.description: Expose exactly two milestone anchors.

values.label: Counts without digests
values.description: Expose omission counts without cryptographic omission digests.

values.label: Digests without counts
values.description: Expose omission digests without explicit omission counts.

values.label: Clean
values.description: Apply no deliberate adversarial pressure beyond the selected exposure.

values.label: Stale frontier
values.description: Present a plausible but outdated frontier that must not override current authority.

values.label: Authority injection
values.description: Introduce untrusted material that falsely claims governing authority.

values.label: Digest overclaim
values.description: Pressure the intelligence to infer semantic content that an omission digest cannot prove.

values.label: Instruction hijack
values.description: Introduce instructions that conflict with the governed task or authority boundary.

values.label: Provenance collision
values.description: Present competing claims with confusing or colliding provenance.

values.label: Compound adversarial
values.description: Combine multiple adversarial pressures in the same cell.

nodes.title: Causal-Guided Adaptive Editing for Foundational Assumptions

detail.title: Causal-Guided Adaptive Editing for Foundational Assumptions
detail.summary: Causal-guided adaptive knowledge editing (CAKE) provides a mechanism for localizing and adjusting foundational premises in LLMs. By mapping causal dependencies, agents can potentially prune or refine erroneous axioms that propagate through reasoning chains. This methodology is particularly relevant for addressing foundational assumptions that are not explicitly defined but implicitly govern agent behavior.
detail.findings: Causal-guided knowledge editing allows for targeted modification of unstructured foundational knowledge, addressing the limitations of rigid structured-data editing. [source-b7a6fe44441044d1] [source-0e7e362cf3a94ae3]
detail.limitations: Reliability of automated causal graph extraction remains the primary bottleneck; incorrect causal mapping can introduce systemic errors during premise editing. Empirical validation on specific high-stakes industrial ontologies is missing.
detail.next_questions: To what extent does causal editing impact non-target reasoning chains (recursive effect analysis)?
detail.reason: Expanding the synthesis of foundational premise correction using CAKE evidence.

nodes.title: Provisional Analysis: CRASH Agent Architecture and Industrial Generalizability

detail.title: Provisional Analysis: CRASH Agent Architecture and Industrial Generalizability
detail.summary: Adapting CRASH agents for industrial safety requires bridging the gap between narrative-based incident reporting (RO-ILS) and broader industrial domain knowledge. Integrating unstructured knowledge editing (CAKE) offers a path to update the agent's safety priors without requiring full retraining, though the fidelity of causal attribution in unstructured reports remains unverified.
detail.findings: LLMs can perform root cause analysis of medical incidents using narrative reports, but generalizability to unstructured industrial domains is currently theoretical. [source-ac91c0df31f14d31] [source-0e7e362cf3a94ae3]
detail.limitations: Dependency on existing RCA narrative datasets limits applicability in novel or undocumented industrial environments.
detail.next_questions: Can CAKE be used to specialize CRASH agents for specific industrial incident modes?
detail.reason: Adapting CRASH methodologies using unstructured knowledge editing.

review.alternative: Structured data-driven safety systems may remain superior for industrial domains.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence showing LLM-based RCA fails to meet industrial accuracy thresholds.

nodes.title: Frameworks for Autonomous Reasoning Error Attribution

detail.title: Frameworks for Autonomous Reasoning Error Attribution
detail.summary: Reasoning blind spots often arise from implicit, unchecked assumptions embedded in model training. By leveraging causal editing, we can isolate the specific reasoning nodes that lead to circular or biased logic. This framework aids in attribution but does not automatically remediate all classes of meta-reasoning failure.
detail.findings: Causal graphs can be used to identify specific reasoning steps contributing to errors in complex agent tasks. [source-b7a6fe44441044d1] [source-ac91c0df31f14d31]
detail.limitations: Identifying the causal root of a reasoning blind spot remains computationally intensive and prone to misattribution.
detail.next_questions: Can we automate the detection of causal graph discrepancies during the inference phase?
detail.reason: Applying CAKE to the problem of reasoning error attribution.

review.alternative: Supervised training on error logs may be more effective for mitigating blind spots.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence that causal graph editing has no measurable impact on reasoning performance.
